commits.message:
docs(protocol): hand implementors the parser the width contract requires

The page asserted a contract and withheld the only tool that satisfies
it. `withCellWidth` was not exported, so its `MyWidget` example clamped
with `Math.min(10, options.maxWidth)` — which is `NaN` for a NaN width,
the exact bug the epic fixed internally, demonstrated as the pattern to
copy two paragraphs above the rule forbidding it.

`withCellWidth` joins the barrel and the example calls it. The
alternative — printing an inline `Number.isFinite(...) ? ... : 0` in the
prose — was refused: it mints a second copy of the parse rule where
nothing checks it against `cellCount`, which is this finding's own
failure mode one layer down. It already disagreed, mapping `Infinity` to
zero. `cellCount` itself stays internal; `withCellWidth(options).maxWidth`
is the ceiling a `measure` needs, and two doors onto one rule is how the
rule starts having two answers.

Exporting it is not merely convenient. The width checkpoint sits at each
render/measure entry because `render()` is public and every entry is a
real crossing — and a third-party `Renderable` is one of those entries.
The page also now says that nothing calls it on the implementor's
behalf, since `renderToString` forwards `options?.width` untouched.

`Infinity` was claimed as "not a supported width" beside a `cellCount`
comment calling an unbounded width "a legitimate request", which passes
it through unchanged. Two maps, one fact, opposite readings — and
neither was the territory: nothing in `src/` passes `Infinity` as a
maxWidth, `Table` modelling its own unboundedness as a deliberately
finite `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. Both texts now say what happens — it passes
the checkpoint unclamped, and the renderables that throw on it are the
open `rich-width-3cf.5` gap, not something the contract prevents. No
clamp was added, because there is no cell count that means unbounded and
picking one here would answer that ticket behind a checkpoint change.

Per test/coverage, the new value export needs a demo rather than an
allowlist entry, and `examples/shared/window.ts` is a custom renderable
that was breaking this very contract: its `measure` returned
`MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` regardless of the offer, a ceiling no parent could
divide against. It now parses and reports the offer, so the page's
worked example and the shipped one agree. Verified the gate by removing
the demo and watching it name the export.

fix(columns): parse a declared column width as the cell count it is

`Columns.render` parses `options.maxWidth` through `withCellWidth`, but
`this.colWidth` arrives by a different door — the constructor — and was
used raw. `new Columns(items, { width: NaN })` made `Math.max(1, NaN)` a
NaN column count and `new Array(NaN)` threw `RangeError: Invalid array
length` before a single column was laid out. `width: 4.5` laid out
fractional columns.

Same rule, same parser, applied where that door is: `cellCount` in the
constructor, as `Table` does for `col.width` via `demandCells`. Absence
is preserved rather than parsed — `undefined` selects auto-fit, and
`cellCount(undefined)` would read it as a declared zero and silently
reroute an auto Columns into the declared-width branch.

The tests live in columns.test.ts rather than the width sweep because a
Columns with a declared `width` legitimately overruns a narrower
`options.maxWidth`, the way a declared-width Table does
(`rich-table-width-y1a`), so the sweep's upper bound is the wrong
assertion for it. What does hold is the equivalence the sweep pins
elsewhere, asserted against a reference render: a declared NaN, -5 and
4.5 lay out as 0, 0 and 4. All three fail against the previous commit.

fix(padding): divide the requested width once, so no row can overflow it

`Padding` had the defect the rest of this epic fixed, and the sweep this
branch adds did not cover it — so it shipped a guard with a hole where
one of the renderables it guards used to be.

It derived its geometry three times and clamped each derivation
differently. `render` took the canvas as `Math.max(1, maxWidth - left -
right)`, which clamps *up*: a padding of 1 inside a 2-cell request drew
3-cell content rows beside 2-cell blank rows, an open frame the terminal
then soft-wraps. `blankLine` came off the raw `maxWidth`, so a negative
width reached `" ".repeat` and threw `RangeError: Invalid count value:
-5` — publicly reachable as `renderToString(new Padding(x, 1), { width:
-5 })`. `measure` derived it a third time and reported a range past the
offer in both directions:

    Padding.measure({maxWidth: -5})           {minimum: 2, maximum: -5}
    new Padding(x, 3).measure({maxWidth: 2})  {minimum: 8, maximum: 8}

`layoutPadding` now divides the requested width once into left, content
and right, summing to exactly it, with `cellCount` at that single
division point. Content takes its first cell before padding takes any,
matching `layoutPanel`: a squeeze should cost the decoration, not the
thing being decorated. `render` and `measure` both read that division,
so they cannot disagree again.

Content rows route through `Segment.adjustLineLength`, whose `pad` flag
is exactly what `expand` means — while its crop half runs unconditionally,
so a child that ignored the canvas it was handed cannot burst the padding
around it. That replaces the hand-rolled `remaining` arithmetic, and the
zero-length spans it leaves behind need no branch to suppress, since the
wire boundary drops empty segments.

Three `Padding` configurations join the sweep. Eleven of their twelve
assertions fail against the previous commit; the twelfth is the ragged
shape's deliberate no-op.

docs(protocol): state what a width means, once (rich-width-3cf.3)

`docs/protocol.md` described `RenderOptions.maxWidth` only as "width and other
context", so an author of a custom renderable had nowhere to learn what the
number means at the bottom of its range — which is the regime the whole
`rich-width-3cf` epic lives in.

It now says: a count of cells, every emitted line fits inside it, a negative
width and NaN both mean zero, a fractional width is floored, zero is a real
request, and `measure` carries the same ceiling.

The `MyWidget` example is fixed in the same pass because it taught the defect:
`return new Measurement(10, 40)` ignores `options.maxWidth` entirely and
reports a minimum above its own maximum as soon as the offer drops below 10.
That is exactly the bug `Columns` and `Layout` had, and a reader copying the
example inherited it.

test(width): sweep every renderable across the widths nobody tests (rich-width-3cf.3)

The standing guard for the epic: one sweep, applied to a table of fifteen
configurations across Panel, Table, Tree, Columns and Layout, asserting that
none of them emits a line wider than the width it was given at any width from
0 to 20 — and that a fractional or non-numeric width renders exactly as its
floor.

The sweep found that three of the five renderables did not hold, so this
commit also makes them hold.

WHAT THE ASSERTIONS ARE FOR. Each is here because a bound alone was measured
to miss a real bug. A renderable that emits nothing satisfies "no line exceeds
the width" — `RichText` with the default `ellipsis` overflow emitted zero
lines at maxWidth 1, which is why a hard-squeezed table looked blank rather
than truncated. A broken frame's content rows are narrower than its border,
not wider — padding 1.5 on a Panel gave [13, 11, 13]. And a width that is not
an integer corrupts output without exceeding anything. So: at least one line,
rows that agree for renderables that draw a frame, a measured range a parent
can divide, and equality against a reference render.

THE ONE SENTENCE THE CODE NEVER SAID. Every failure was the same fact stated
nowhere: maxWidth is a count of cells, so a non-negative integer. `table.ts`
said it in `cells()`, `padding.ts` said it again in `side()`, `panel.ts`
approximated it with `Math.max(1, ...)`, and `text.ts`, `tree.ts`,
`columns.ts` and `layout.ts` never said it at all — so they disagreed. At NaN,
Table collapsed to one cell of garbage, Columns and Layout threw `Invalid
array length`, and RichText ignored the request and emitted its full natural
width.

Now `cellCount` in `core/cells.ts` is the only place that rule lives, and
`withCellWidth` in `core/protocol.ts` is the checkpoint every renderable
crosses. It returns options rather than a number on purpose: parsing into a
local leaves the caller's raw value in `options` for whatever the renderable
forwards it to. Columns was fixed that way first and still threw, because it
handed the unparsed original to `Measurement.get`.

The two RichText questions the ticket asked to be decided once:

- fold into a zero-cell canvas emits the bare line terminator, the same as
  crop and ellipsis, instead of stepping by zero forever (~2^27 pushes and a
  gigabyte before a RangeError).
- ellipsis at maxWidth 1 emits the marker. The `maxWidth > 1` guard that stood
  there was a guard with no else over arithmetic that was already correct at
  1; deleting it is the whole fix.

Tree had the epic's defect verbatim: it emitted its guides and then handed the
label `options` unchanged, so the label was told it had the whole outer width
while the guides had already spent four cells of it. Both call sites now route
through one `_renderRow` that divides the width once. Layout applied each
child's `minimumSize` independently of the budget, so two children asked to
fit one cell merged into a two-cell row.

`maxWidth: Infinity` is deliberately outside the sweep and still throws in
Panel, Columns and Layout. The epic's invariant is trivially true there, and
the crash is an expansion defect rather than a squeeze; deciding what every
renderable renders at an unbounded width is worth doing on purpose, so it is
filed rather than smuggled in behind a clamp.

fix(table): divide the requested width once, so no row can overflow it (rich-width-3cf.2) (#77)

* fix(table): divide the requested width once, so no row can overflow it (rich-width-3cf.2)

`Table` emitted rows at a width it picked without reference to the width it was
given. At every requested width from 1 to 13 the sample three-column table
rendered the same 13 cells, because the width was divided in three independent
places that could not agree: `_calculateWidths` subtracted borders and padding,
`_totalTableWidth` added them back, and five box-row callsites re-derived
`w + padLeft + padRight`. The `Math.max(1, ...)` floor in the first pinned every
column at one cell while the other two kept billing for padding that was no
longer affordable. The terminal soft-wraps such a row, and the wrap destroys the
frame of every renderable printed after it.

One `layoutTable(outerWidth, demands, padding, frame)` now returns fields that
sum to exactly the width it produced, and that width is never more than the one
requested. Every row reads from it: both borders, the header separator, the
section and footer rules, the data rows, and the title/caption spans.

Cells go out in the same priority order `Panel` uses — the pair of edge columns,
then one content cell per column with the divider in front of it, then the
padding, then the remainder back to content. A column the width cannot seat is
dropped rather than drawn outside the frame.

The remainder is apportioned a cell at a time by the highest-averages rule
rather than by proportional flooring, so the granted widths are exact with no
rounding residue for a second pass to sweep up, and per-column caps fall out for
free: a capped column stops winning rounds and its cells flow to the columns
that can use them. A declared `width` is a reservation paid before the bidding
rather than a weight competing in it — without that distinction a wide neighbour
wins every cell and a `width: 4` column renders one cell wide.

Also fixed, both found by following the geometry through:

- `measure({ maxWidth: 1 })` returned `{minimum: 6, maximum: 1}` — a floor above
  its own ceiling. Both ends are now widths the geometry produced, so the range
  cannot invert.
- `_renderTitle` cropped by code units, so a title of wide characters was up to
  twice the table's width on screen. It crops by cells now.

`Box.getTop`/`getRow`/`getBottom` take `readonly number[]`; they never mutated
the array, and dropping the constraint beats copying at four callsites.

Not changed here: `expand` is still accepted and unimplemented — wiring it up
needs `Progress` to put a ratio on its bar column first, or every progress row
gets three equal columns. Filed separately.

* fix(table): bound the width apportionment by column count, not by the width

`distribute` handed out cells one at a time, so its iteration count was the
requested width. A `ratio` column never reaches a cap, which left the loop
draining the budget alone — and `Infinity - 1 === Infinity`, so a table with a
ratio column and a `maxWidth` of `Infinity` looped forever. Both
`TableOptions.width` and `RenderOptions.maxWidth` are plain numbers with nothing
stopping that value, and a silent hang is worse than the `RangeError` the
arithmetic this replaced would have produced.

The apportionment is now closed-form: a column whose proportional share would
overshoot its cap is granted its want and dropped, its unused cells are reopened
to the rest, and that repeats until everyone still open fits within their share.
One largest-remainder pass then places the cells the shares left as fractions,
so the widths still sum exactly. Each round caps at least one column or is the
last, so the work is bounded by the number of columns.

Rejecting non-finite widths at the boundary would have been the smaller change
and the wrong one: an ordinary table already renders correctly at
`maxWidth: Infinity` — every bounded column caps at its natural width and there
is nothing left to apportion — so a guard would have traded a hang for a
regression. There is a test pinning that case now.

The docblock's claim that one-at-a-time allocation left "no rounding residue for
a second pass to sweep up" stopped being true with this change, so it is gone
rather than left standing next to the second pass.

docs: the narrow-widths ladder labelled a column "width 11" while showing the
width-10 render. A padding level is bought for every column at once or not at
all, so 10, 11 and 12 are one plateau and no width-11 rendering of that example
exists. The ladder now uses widths whose render lands exactly on the request, so
counting characters confirms each label, and says what happens in between.

* fix(table): let a column that wants no cells have none

The seating pass handed every seated column an unconditional first content cell,
and `Math.max(1, ...)` floors in the demand computation made sure no column
could ask for fewer. A zero-width spacer therefore gained a cell it never asked
for: `width: 0` next to a normal column rendered `+---+` where a6c38ef rendered
`+--+`.

The floor reached further than a declared width. `_naturalWidth` carried the
same `Math.max(1, ...)`, so a column with no header and no content changed
identically — and a `Table.grid()` used as a gutter is far more likely to take
that path than an explicit `width: 0`.

The seat is now `Math.min(1, want)`. The queue exists to stop one column taking
a second cell before another has its first, and a column that wants nothing has
no place in it; the reservation and apportionment arithmetic that assumed a seat
of 1 is taken net of the seat instead. Spacers pay their divider and padding and
nothing more, which is what they did before the rewrite.

One deliberate difference from a6c38ef: a negative declared width floors at 0
rather than reaching `" ".repeat(-1)` and throwing. That is the rule #76 already
established for the same class of input, where `normalizePadding` floors every
side at zero as it is parsed.

* fix(table): floor a non-finite width where it enters the layout

`Math.max(0, n)` returns NaN for a NaN input, so a caller's `width: NaN` — a
plausible `total / count` with a zero count — did not merely mis-size its own
column. It reached `budget -= NaN` in the seating pass, and from there every
`budget < cost` comparison was false, because comparisons against NaN always
are. The bounds check was not wrong, it was switched off: every remaining
column got seated regardless of the space, padding and reservations came back
NaN for the whole table, and `" ".repeat(NaN)` renders as `""` rather than
throwing. A two-column table collapsed to `+++` silently.

The same value arrives through three doors — the requested `outerWidth`, a
column's declared `width`, and the `minWidth`/`maxWidth` bounding a natural
width — so it is normalized once at each, rather than guarded at the dozen
comparisons downstream that would otherwise have to survive it.

`n > 0 ? n : 0` rather than `Number.isFinite(n) ? ... : ...`: the comparison
already rejects NaN, since NaN fails every comparison, and it floors negatives
with the same expression it replaces. `Infinity` passes through, which an
unbounded width needs. That is also why a NaN `ratio` needs nothing here —
`distribute` admits a column to its working set on `weight > 0`, which has
excluded NaN all along.

Flooring rather than throwing is the rule already set for out-of-domain numbers
here: #76 floors negative padding as it is parsed, and this branch floors a
negative declared width for the same reason.

* fix(table): measure against the width the container offered

`measure()` laid both ends of its range out against `this.tableWidth ?? maxWidth`,
but `Measurement.get` clamps only the maximum it gets back and passes the
minimum through untouched. A table with a declared width wider than the space it
was being measured in therefore reported a floor computed against the declared
width and a ceiling clamped to the offered one — `{minimum: 13, maximum: 5}` for
three columns measured at `maxWidth: 5`.

That is the same inverted range this method's docblock says is no longer
possible. The claim was true of `outerWidth` and false of the width the caller
actually offered, which is the one the range is read against. Bounding
`outerWidth` by `options.maxWidth` makes it true as written.

The double `_columnDemands()` call goes with it. Both layouts derive from one
array now; the second call only ever recomputed it, and it re-walks every row of
every natural column through `_naturalWidth` to do so — on the entry point
`Layout` and `Columns` hit repeatedly while probing candidate widths.

Scoped to `measure()`. `render()` also lays out at the declared width and does
overflow a narrower container, but a6c38ef does that too, so it is long-standing
behaviour of a documented option rather than anything this branch introduced.
Filed as rich-table-width-y1a.

* docs(tables): correct three claims the renderer does not honour

The ladder omitted width 4, and the sentence under it generalizes from the
listed rungs — so "in between it sits on the previous rung" read as a claim
about width 4 that is false: at width 4 only one column is seated, a padding
level therefore costs one cell, and the single leftover cell can afford it.
Width 4 lands exactly on the request and is a rung by the paragraph's own
definition. Listing it makes the existing sentence true for every width from 2
to 16, checked by rendering each one, rather than needing an exception written
beside it. The figure is regenerated from the renderer, which is how the
"width 11" mislabel on this branch was caught.

A declared-`width` column did not "keep its size and its neighbours absorb the
shortfall". Reservations are paid after the frame, the seats and the padding, so
a width too small to cover them shrinks reserved columns too: `width: 5` beside
a natural column renders at one content cell when the table is asked for 8. The
ordering is deliberate — cell priority is `Panel`'s and Python Rich's — so the
claim is corrected to what the renderer does.

Correcting the `expand` row to say it is not wired into sizing left the Grids
section still presenting `Table.grid({ expand: true })` as the way to fill the
terminal. One file said both; the example silently no-ops. It now points at the
sizing note. Wiring `expand` remains rich-table-rrz.

The opening claim is narrowed to a table with no declared `width`, which is the
only shape it holds for: an explicit width overrides a narrower container, and
that is now stated on the option itself.

* fix(padding): floor a non-finite side where padding is parsed

`normalizePadding` floored each side with `Math.max(0, n)`, which returns NaN
unchanged, so its docblock's guarantee — that past this crossing
`" ".repeat(left)` is safe in any renderable without asking what the caller
passed — held for negative sides and not for NaN. `new Table({ padding: NaN })`
collapsed a two-column table to `+++`: `takePerColumn` returned NaN, and
`budget -= per * seated` then made every later bounds check false, since
comparisons against NaN always are.

The floor belongs here rather than at the callsite that found it. Running
`layoutTable`'s destructured sides through the table's own normalizer would
have left `Padding` and `Panel` taking the same NaN through the same door, and
put a second floor for one invariant a layer below the one that already owns it.

* fix(table): keep an infinite bound out of the demand model

`cells()` lets `Infinity` through, which is right where it normalizes the
requested outer width — an unbounded width is deliberate and tested. Reusing it
to build column demands let that value into a model with no room for it:
`UNBOUNDED` is this model's own infinity, and a literal `Infinity` reaching
`distribute` makes a column's weighted share `Infinity / Infinity`, which is
NaN. The NaN then skews every other elastic column, so `minWidth: Infinity`
rendered a 7-cell border above a 9-cell row — the frame broken, not merely one
column mis-sized. `ratio: Infinity` did the same, since both `flexible` and the
elastic branch ask only for `ratio > 0`.

`demandCells` caps at `UNBOUNDED` so a `ColumnDemand` is finite by
construction, and it is applied in all three branches that build one. Mapping
`Infinity` onto `UNBOUNDED` says the intended thing in the vocabulary the model
already has rather than adding a second one.

`distribute`'s `open` filter is deliberately untouched. `weight > 0` is what
has always made a NaN weight harmless, and adding `Number.isFinite` beside it
would guard against a state the constructor no longer produces.

`_naturalWidth` now returns its bounded value unfloored: the floor moved to the
demand it feeds, and keeping both would be two enforcers for one rule.

* test(table): name the NaN-width test after the path it takes

`NaN !== undefined`, so a NaN column `width` takes the declared-width branch and
becomes a declared width of zero — the same demand an explicit `width: 0`
produces. The title claimed it was treated as no declared width, which would
mean falling through to natural sizing and rendering the cell's own content; the
assertion it sits above says otherwise.

The code and `eef1a2f`'s message were already accurate. Only the name
overclaimed, and a name is read as a description of the behaviour whether or not
it is true of it.

* fix(padding): truncate a fractional side where padding is parsed

A cell is not divisible, and `normalizePadding` enforced only the non-negative
half of that domain. A fractional side reached `" ".repeat`, which truncates,
while the box rows around it are measured arithmetically — so `padding: 1.5`
drew 13-cell borders around an 11-cell content row and the frame did not close.

Flooring here rather than at either callsite keeps the guarantee the docblock
already makes: past this crossing a side is a count of cells, so no renderer
downstream has to ask what the caller wrote. `Padding` and `Panel` take the
same crossing and had the same break.

* fix(table): buy whole cells only, whatever width was requested

`cells()` enforced the non-negative half of a cell count's domain and not the
integral half, so a fractional `outerWidth` — `new Table({ width: 10.5 })`, or a
`maxWidth` computed by a caller — left `budget` fractional for the whole layout.
It reached `distribute`'s largest-remainder pass, which tops columns up a whole
cell at a time against a `residue` that was itself fractional, so a residue of
0.5 still bought a full cell. A table asked for 10.5 emitted 11, and 9.5, 7.25
and 3.5 all overshot the same way — the one invariant this branch exists to
hold.

Flooring at the parse point rather than at the top of `distribute` makes that
function's integer assumption true instead of defended, and it is the only place
that catches the same value on its way to the padding and the box rows;
`distribute` is where the overshoot surfaced, not where it entered.

`Infinity` survives `Math.floor`, so the unbounded-width path is unchanged.
